prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) give a tractable dynamic mechanism in which a small shock to collateral values is amplified and propagated into persistent fluctuations in credit and output. It became the foundation for later macro-finance models of financial frictions, and the 2007-09 crisis made its relevance concrete for policy. Attribution is the cleanest of the shortlisted macro candidates, because the core idea sits in one two-author paper and a two-name prize follows directly from it. The work is nearly three decades old, so there has been time for extension, quantitative use and criticism. Having read my colleagues' openings, I still rank it first, but with less confidence than before, mainly because of the strength of the macro and labour alternatives.
statement.case_against: The contribution is theory-led, and direct empirical identification of the specific collateral-amplification channel is more mixed than the model's influence suggests. Much of the post-2008 support shows that financial frictions matter, which is not the same as validating this mechanism. The adjacent financial-accelerator literature (Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist) overlaps with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which weakens the marginal case. Compared with B015 and B036, the breadth of policy and empirical use is narrower.

responses.point: Ranks B015 first because nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin central-bank practice, and the framework has been tested through several policy regimes and episodes.
responses.response: I agree the practical influence of B015 is very large and the maturity is not in doubt. My hesitation is attribution. Your own opening says at least eight credited names have claims, and that omitting Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost. A prize that credits the framework to three people risks misdescribing how the field was built. I also do not know whether the framework's performance in the post-2021 inflation counts as a pass or a partial failure, and I would want that settled before ranking it above a contribution with a clean credit set. I have therefore not put B015 in my own top positions, and I would rather say so than treat its breadth of influence as settling the credit question.

responses.point: Also ranks B050 first and restricts it to Kiyotaki and Moore. He notes that Gertler, Gilchrist and the accelerator line are partly covered by the 2022 prize to Bernanke, and that direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is mixed.
responses.response: I share both points and they drive my two-name proposal. I would go further on the empirical concern. As a metascience-minded reader, I would want evidence that targets the collateral-constraint channel itself and does not merely show that credit frictions matter after 2008. I treat this as the main weakness of B050, and it is why I hold the case with some humility. It does not undo the foundational contribution, but the committee should be careful not to cite the post-crisis literature as validation of this specific mechanism.

responses.point: Proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler for B050. She sees Gertler's financial-accelerator and intermediary-frictions work as closely related, while noting that the 2022 prize weakens the accelerator side.
responses.response: I take the point that Gertler's work is closely related, and your own caveat about the 2022 prize is the reason I would leave him out. His accelerator contribution is part of a lineage whose central figure, Bernanke, is already recognised and is not on this ballot. He also appears on B015, so adding him to B050 blurs what the prize is for. I think a citation about the collateral-constraint mechanism is better served by the two originators. I could be persuaded if the committee wants a broader macro-finance prize, but then the credit logic would need to be stated explicitly.

responses.point: Ranks B036 first, arguing that the task framework combined with credible local-labour-market identification of the trade shock has had very large research and policy influence and is now well tested.
responses.response: This is the candidate I find strongest on empirical credibility, which is why it is my second choice. The quasi-experimental design is the kind of evidence I weight heavily. I qualify it on two points you also raise: the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock estimates are still debated, and the task framework draws on contributors outside the credited names, notably Acemoglu, who is already a laureate. The bundling of two strands with partly different authorship also makes a three-name set imperfect, and Dorn's omission would be hard to defend. I see B036 as a close alternative but not a clearer case on attribution than B050.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the collateral-constraint mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the financial-accelerator work recognised through the 2022 prize.
How much weight to give the direct empirical identification of the collateral channel, as against the broader post-crisis evidence on financial frictions.
Whether the diffuse credit in B015 should count against it as strongly as I have assumed, given its breadth of policy use.
How to apportion credit in B036 between the task framework and the China-shock evidence, and whether Dorn should be included.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and I have not independently verified the record.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Her co-authors and institutional ties (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johannesson, the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network and Brodeur) do not appear among the credited names for any shortlisted ballot ID.
